prompt: A bakery chain is building an operational decision system. Sort each component by the discipline that does the work.

cards.text: Estimating how many croissants each store will sell on Sunday
cards.explanation: Sunday demand is an uncertain quantity estimated from data, which is prediction.

cards.text: Estimating how many days the flour supplier's next truck will take to arrive
cards.explanation: Transit time is uncertain, so the model estimates it from past deliveries.

cards.text: Choosing which batches each oven bakes, given that each oven holds only 12 trays
cards.explanation: Picking a schedule that respects a hard capacity limit is the solver's job.

cards.text: Assigning orders to delivery vans so that no van exceeds its weight limit
cards.explanation: The weight limit is a hard physical constraint that optimization enforces.

cards.text: Estimating the chance that a dough mixer breaks down this month
cards.explanation: A failure probability is an uncertain quantity, which is prediction.

cards.text: Setting the bakers' shift plan so that nobody works more than 10 hours
cards.explanation: Shift labor rules are constraints, and the plan that respects them is a prescription.

question_text: Two brands of umbrella each sell an average of 60 units a week at a store. For brand A, the 90th percentile of weekly demand is 66 units. For brand B, it is 110 units. The manager wants a 10 percent stockout risk for each brand. What should the store stock?

options.option_text: 60 units of each brand, because the average demand is the same
options.option_explanation: Stocking the average ignores volatility. Brand B would run out far more often than 10 percent of weeks.

options.option_text: 110 units of each brand, to be safe
options.option_explanation: Brand A only needs 66 units for a 10 percent stockout risk. The extra stock would tie up capital.

options.option_text: 66 units of A and 110 units of B
options.option_explanation: Correct. Stocking each brand to its own 90th percentile covers demand in 90 percent of weeks and leaves a 10 percent stockout risk.

options.option_text: 88 units of each brand, the average of the two percentiles
options.option_explanation: Averaging the percentiles overstocks the steady brand and understocks the volatile one.

question_text: A florist sells roses for Valentine's Day. Each rose left unsold loses $1 (it wilts). Each customer turned away costs $3 in lost margin. At which percentile of predicted demand should the florist stock?

options.option_text: The 25th percentile, because unsold roses are wasted
options.option_explanation: That fraction is Co / (Cu + Co). The critical fractile puts the underage cost on top: 3 / (3 + 1).
Correct. The critical fractile is 3 / (3 + 1) = 0.75, so the florist stocks to the 75th percentile.
Stocking the median is right only when underage and overage cost the same. Here running short costs three times as much.

options.option_text: The 100th percentile, so no customer is ever turned away
options.option_explanation: Covering every possible customer would leave many wilted roses. The best quantity balances the two costs.

prompt: A grocery delivery service runs dynamic routing for one afternoon. Put the steps in the order they happen.

steps.text: Models trained on past GPS traces predict driving time for each street segment and service time at each address
steps.explanation: The solver needs realistic travel and drop-off times before it can plan anything.

steps.text: The solver assigns orders to vans and sequences the stops within each customer's time window
steps.explanation: With the predictions as inputs, the solver produces the first plan.

steps.text: A crash closes a bridge and a customer adds a last-minute order
steps.explanation: Something changes after the vans have left the depot.

steps.text: The travel-time predictions for the affected segments are updated
steps.explanation: The new conditions must reach the inputs before the plan can change.

steps.text: The solver re-solves the routes and sends new stop sequences to the drivers
steps.explanation: Dynamic routing re-solves the problem during the day with the updated inputs.

prompt: For each case, name the maintenance paradigm being used.

cases.text: A building replaces its elevator cables every 18 months, whatever their condition.
cases.explanation: A fixed calendar schedule, regardless of actual wear, is preventive maintenance.

cases.text: An office fixes its printer only after it jams and stops working.
cases.explanation: Running the machine until it breaks is reactive maintenance.

cases.text: A rail operator uses wheel vibration data to estimate each train's remaining useful life and books repairs for the weekend before the estimated failure.
cases.explanation: Sensor data and a model estimate the health of each specific asset, which is predictive maintenance.

cases.text: A delivery fleet changes engine oil every 10,000 kilometres.
cases.explanation: A fixed interval of use, not measured wear, sets the timing.

cases.text: A data centre sees a cooling fan's motor current drifting from its normal pattern and swaps that one fan during a planned window.
cases.explanation: The swap is triggered by the measured health of that specific fan.

question_text: A bottling plant wants a camera system to find cracked glass bottles. Cracks appear in about 1 bottle in 20,000, so the plant has thousands of images of good bottles but only a handful of cracked ones. What is the most sensible way to train the detector?

options.option_text: Train a standard classifier on the images as they are
options.option_explanation: With so few cracked examples, the classifier can score well by calling every bottle good. That is the class imbalance problem.

options.option_text: Send the images to a cloud model and wait for its answer
options.option_explanation: Cloud processing does not solve the lack of defect images, and the round trip is too slow to trigger a reject gate at line speed.

options.option_text: Wait until a thousand cracked bottles have been photographed
options.option_explanation: At 1 in 20,000, that would take millions of bottles, with defects shipping to customers in the meantime.

options.option_text: Train an anomaly model on the many good-bottle images and flag anything unusual
options.option_explanation: Correct. Learning what a defect-free part looks like works even when defect examples are rare. Synthesizing crack images is another option.

prompt: A pharmacy chain lets replenishment agents order directly from wholesalers. Sort each control by whether it is a hard deterministic guardrail outside the model.

cards.text: The ordering system rejects any order above 3 times a store's normal daily quantity
cards.explanation: A maximum daily order-quantity cap is enforced by fixed code, whatever the agent proposes.

cards.text: The agent's instructions ask it to avoid panic buying
cards.explanation: An instruction to the model can be ignored or misread. It is not enforced outside the model.

cards.text: Orders priced more than 15 percent above the contract price are blocked
cards.explanation: A price-variance ceiling is a deterministic rule applied outside the model.

cards.text: An agent may raise its reorder quantity by at most 10 percent per day
cards.explanation: A rate limiter on reorder adjustments slows the spiral regardless of what the agent perceives.

cards.text: The agent is upgraded to a larger language model that forecasts more accurately
cards.explanation: Better forecasts do not stop many agents reacting to the same shortage signal at once.

cards.text: The agent reports how confident it is in each surge order
cards.explanation: A self-reported confidence score comes from the model and blocks nothing on its own.
